Twentieth Indian Expedition to Antarctica, Scientific Report, 2006 
Ministry of Earth Sciences, Technical Publication No. 18, pp 37-51 
Magnetic Pulsations over Antarctica: Results from the 
Three-Station Triangulation Experiment 
S. Gurubaran1, K. Jeeva1, M. Sridharan2, S. Singh3, 
A. Dhar3, A. N. Hanchinal3 and G. Rajaram3 
'Equatorial Geophysical Research Laboratory, Indian Institute of Geomagnetism, 
Krishnapuram, Tirunelveli, 2Magnetic Observatory, Indian Institute of 
Geomagnetism, Pondicherry, 3Indian Institute of Geomagnetism, 
Panvel, Navi Mumbai (e-mail: gurubara@sancharnet.in) 
Abstract 
Results from the magnetic field observations carried out during the summer 
campaign of the XX Indian Antarctic Expedition (2000-2001) are presented in this work. 
Simultaneous data from three locations (Maitri, Dakshin Gangotri and the third near Sigurd 
Mountain) were made use of in order to identify the ground magnetic signatures of the 
distant geospace processes that occurred on 24 January 2001. An isolated pulsation event 
(a westward propagating disturbance) in the Pi3 category was recorded at all the three 
stations during this period. Triangulation of magnetic records reveals velocities of this 
waveform to be ~1 km/s. The present work clearly highlights the importance of continuing 
magnetic field measurements in the icy continent, as space weather is an important area 
that is gaining attention in recent times. 
Keywords: Ionosphere, antarctic geomagnetism, solar wind-magnetosphere 
interactions, currents, magnetic fields. 
Introduction 
The geographical location of Maitri is unique in that under quiet 
geomagnetic conditions the station is under the influence of the mid-
latitude ionospheric Sq current system. As the magnetic disturbances grow 
due to the enhanced solar wind-magnetosphere interaction, the atmosphere 
over Maitri comes increasingly under the auroral oval. The auroral oval 
expands under such conditions to envelop the sky over Maitri. 
Past experiments conducted at the Indian Antarctic station clearly 
distinguished the disturbed time behaviour of the geomagnetic field 
variations from their quiet-time characteristics (Kalra et al. 1995, for 
example). Many important processes occur on the nightside of the Earth 
wherein the geomagnetic field is stretched to form a long 'tail' by the 
38 S. Gurubaran et al. 
streaming charged particle flow from the Sun. The field lines forming the 
tail are 'energized' whenever the interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) turns 
southward as this favours magnetic field reconnection on the dayside of 
the Earth. The reconnected field is swept across towards the nightside. 
The magnetic field ultimately releases the energy in the form of sporadic 
bursts in the tail region that manifest as substorms in the ground 
geomagnetic data (see McPherron 1991, for a review on magnetospheric 
substorms). The channel in which this energy is routed through is the 
substorm current wedge that takes a westward path in the high latitude 
ionosphere. Field-aligned currents constitute the edges of this current 
pattern (Kisabeth & Rostoker 1973, for example). Simultaneously, the 
energy extracted from the solar wind may be dissipated in the ionosphere 
through the directly driven process leading to an enhancement of the 
convection driven auroral electrojets in the dawn and dusk sectors 
(Rostoker 1999, for a recent review). This process coincides with the 
growth phase of a magnetospheric substorm. 
The Indian Institute of Geomagnetism (IIG) continues to operate 
fluxgate magnetometers at the Indian Antarctic station, Maitri (70°45' S, 
11°45'E, geographic; 66°S, 53°21E, geomagnetic). A proton precession 
magnetometer and a riometer have also been operational for quite some 
time at this station. 
The present work focuses on the electrodynamic conditions prevalent 
on 24 January 2001 when there was an opportunity to conduct a 3-station 
triangulation experiment for monitoring the movement of auroral current 
loops. Intense geomagnetic activity was recorded on this day (ZKp = 26") 
with moderate storms observed at mid and low latitudes. 
Geomagnetic pulsations were recorded during this campaign at three 
locations separated from each other by 100-200 km distance, which is the 
scale size of the Hall current loop drifting with the auoral surge. Apart 
from Maitri, fluxgate magnetometers were operated at Dakshin Gangotri 
(70°05'S, 12°E) and a third station near Sigurd Mountain (71°20'S, 
7°38'E). A triangulation of magnetic field variations at these stations 
provided information about the velocity of the mobile current systems. 
Appropriate cross correlation analysis has been performed to quantify the 
results that compare well with earlier results (Kalra et al., 1998, Rajaram 
et al., 2002). Using traditional power spectral analysis, the period of the 
dominant pulsation is identified.
